2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can be stated thus the present petitioner as pre-emptor filed the original preemption miscellaneous case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 against the pre-emptee and others in the Court of learned Senior Assistant Judge, Gournadi, Barisal contending inter alia that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer in the case holding by way of inheritance and purchase. The pre-emptor came to learn about the case kabala for the first time on 26-5-2012. The opposite parties No.2-4 have transferred the case land secretly in favour of the pre-emptee-opposite party No.1 without giving any notice to the pre-emptor-petitioner and thereafter; the pre-emptor collecting the certified copy of the deed in question on 28-5-2012, knowing finally about the sale in respect of the case land measuring 10 (ten) decimals at a consideration of Taka 3,00,000 (Three lac) filed the original case Apr getting the case land pre-empted under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 as the purchaser-opposite party No.1 is a stranger to the case jote. 

 3. After service of summon-notice in the original case the pre- emptee-opposite party No.1 made his appearance and filed an application under Order VII, rule 11(d) along with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the petition for pre-emption stated inter alia that the case is not maintainable in its present form as it is barred under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. It was alleged by the pre-emptee that the nature of the case land is a homestead property and as such the petition for pre-emption is liable to be rejected. 

 9. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that the learned appellate court below during passing the impugned order of rejection of the appeal summarily committed gross illegality and injustice. The learned Advocate further submits that both the courts below have committed error of law resulting in an error in the decisions occasioning failure of justice and as such the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside. The learned Advocate also submits that the courts below have committed an error of law in not considering that the pre-emption case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 is changeable into a pre-emption case under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural of Tenancy Act, 1949. The learned Advocate during his argument submits that section 2(14) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 i.e. the definition of non-agricultural land does not attract the case land and, as such, the pre-emption miscellaneous case filed under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was maintainable. The learned Advocate in his submission pointed out that in the case land there is no existence of any dwelling but or homestead which is badly required for treating the lane as `Non-Agricultural Land', but the learned courts below erred in law as well as in facts and failed to appreciate the contents of the application for pre-emption which is the pleadings of the pre-emptor. Besides this; there is an Advocate Commissioner's report on the application for rejection of the case and the learned Advocate Commissioner in his report clearly mentioned that the land does not exist with homestead and it is a mere ‘Bhiti' land. The learned Advocate lastly submits that for misquoting or non-quoting of appropriate section in the contents of the application for pre-emption the right of pre-emption cannot be curtailed but the learned courts below arbitrarily decided that inasmuch as the original case was a case for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 it is not maintainable and barred by law. 

 10. As against the aforesaid submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties opposing the Rule submits that both the courts below during passing their judgment and order rightly held that the case is not maintainable as it is barred by law. The learned Advocate further submits that there is no illegality or infirmity and non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate submits that the Commissioner's report has no manner of application for consideration in such an application for rejection of plaint. Both the courts below concurrently held that the case land is under the purview of Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act, but since the miscellaneous application for pre-emption is under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act it is barred by law. 

 11. Considering the submissions of the learned Advocates, I have perused the application for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 wherein it has been clearly contended by the pre-emptor-petitioner that the case land was transferred by a saf-kabala deed dated 28-5-2012 and the land measuring 10 decimals was transferred, in favour of the pre-emptee-opposite party No. 1, who is a stranger purchaser at a consideration of Taka 3,00,000 (Taka three lac). The certified copy of the application for pre-emption is annexed herewith as Annexure-`A'. I have also consulted the application under Order VII, rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil' Procedure wherein it was cited by the opposite party No. 1 that the case land being a non-agricultural land and homestead the preemption miscellaneous case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 is not maintainable. With regard to this, having gone through the order passed by the trial court dated 1-9-2015 in pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No. 25 of 2012 and the order of the appellate court dated 30-9-2015 in Miscellaneous Appeal No.64 of 2015 it transpires that the learned District Judge, Barisal held that in the SA Khatian the land transferred, was mentioned as `Bhiti' and `Bagan' and for that reason it can be held that the land is not an agricultural land. In this context; section 2(14) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 defined the homestead in the following way: 

 13. Here in this case, we have come across from the contents of the plaint viz. the application for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act that the description of the property which was transferred in favour of the pre-emptee-opposite party is described as agricultural land. With regard to this, consulting the relevant case kabala being No.671 of 2012 dated 28-5-2012 it appears that in the schedule of the kabala there is a mention of Garden and "Bhita". 

 The facts of the case reported in 27 DLR (AD) 114 is, in short, that the pre-emptor petitioner filed an application under section 96 of the EB SAT Act for pre-emption of certain lands which was contested by the pre-emptee-opposite parties contending, inter alia, that the said land being "chandina land" within a Municipal area the application under section 96 of the Act had no application to the purchase in question. The case was allowed by the trial Court, which was affirmed by the subordinate Judge on appeal, preferred by the pre-emptee-opposite party. He then filed an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the High Court Division and during pendency of the application a petition was filed on behalf of the pre-emptor under Order VI, rule 17 read with section 151 and section 153 of the CPC for amendment of the application for pre-emption whereby the application for pre-emption under section 96 of the SAT Act was sought to be converted to an application under section 24 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act which was rejected by the High Court on the ground that it would change the nature of the case. In an appeal against the said judgment and order by the pre-emptor the Appellate Division held that "In the circumstances we find that the learned judges were not justified in rejecting the prayer for amendment of the application upon the view they took. More-over, since the relief prayed for could be given by the Court under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act even if that section had not been specifically mentioned in the application, it was not necessary either to apply for amendment for a change of description in the cause title. "the Appellate Division also referred a decision reported in (1967) 19 DLR 347, PLD 1967 (Dacca) 588, in its Judgment where it was held that:— 

 "If the relief claimed by the petitioner was allowable under some other law of the country. Namely, section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, then the Court of appeal below was bound to apply the same notwithstanding the mis-description of the cause title in the application." 

 16. In the case of Abdul Majid Pramanik vs Md Sorhab Ali, 16 MLR (AD) 1, our Apex Court held with regard to section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 that the pre-emption of the land of homestead transferred by co-sharer of the tenancy situated in rural areas connected with agricultural, is not maintainable. Similarly, the land situated within municipal area although used for agricultural purpose, is pre-emptable under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. 

 "The pre-emptor wanted to exercise his right of pre-emption in respect of the disputed land on the ground that he was a co-sharer tenant of the tenancy to which the said land appertained. The application was described as one coming under section 96 of the State Acquisition Act. Subsequently when it was realised that having regard to the nature of the disputed land the relief prayed for could be granted under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, an application for amendment to that effect in the cause title of the application with consequential changes was made but the High Court rejected the prayer on the ground inter alia, that the change sought to be made was not "a mere change of one kind of pre-emption to another ", but it was "substitution of a new case altogether." Since a co-sharer tenant of non-agricultural land and is entitled to apply for preemption under section 24 of the Non-agricultural Tenancy Act, it does not appear how the nature and character of the application can be said to be altered by substitution of a new case altogether by reason of the amendment prayed for. Whatever changes were sought to be made were changes in form and not.in substance. In the circumstances we find that the learned Judges were not justified in rejecting the prayer for amendment of the application upon the view they took. Moreover, since the relief prayed for could be given by the court under section 24 of the Non-agricultural Tenancy Act, even if that section had not been specifically mentioned in the application, it was not necessary either to apply for amendment for a change of description in the cause title.
